name: CGBN (CUDA Accelerated Multiple Precision Arithmetic, Cooperative Groups Big Numbers)
baseline: GMP 6.1.2 (mpz) with OpenMP on a 20-core Xeon
workload: Fixed-size unsigned multiple-precision integer operations (add, sub, low mul, Montgomery reduce, odd modular exponentiation, div_qr, sqrt, gcd, modular inverse) on large batches of 128 to 8192-bit operands, Tesla V100 GPU versus all 20 cores of a Xeon running GMP 6.1.2 under OpenMP.
claimed_speedup: Speed-up table in README: add 174.3x at 128 bits down to 28.6x at 8192 bits (avg 77.4x); mul (low) 172.9x down to 14.6x (avg 43.5x); mont_reduce avg 29.3x; powm_odd 22.1x at 128 bits, 16.8x at 8192 bits (avg 21.4x); div_qr avg 14.4x; sqrt avg 11.3x; gcd avg 6.9x; mod inv avg 4.1x.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README (build is 'make <arch>' with CUDA 10+ for Volta and later; GMP compile flags not stated). The perf_tests tools and the gmp-run / gmp-numactl-run make targets that produced the numbers are in the repo.
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 (Volta) GPU versus Intel Xeon E5-2698v4, 20 cores at 2.2 GHz, GMP 6.1.2 with OpenMP
stars_or_usage: 252 stars (NVIDIA Research project; used as the big-number kernel in sethtroisi/prime-gap and other GPU number-theory searches)
tradeoffs: Fixed-size unsigned integers only (32 bits to 32K bits in 32-bit steps), 4/8/16/32 threads cooperate per number, so it needs large batches to fill a GPU; every instance in a kernel has the same bit width; no dynamic allocation; CUDA/NVIDIA only. The README describes it as a beta release (XMP 2.0 beta, Oct 2018).
caveats: Numbers are first-party and from the 2018 beta on a V100 against GMP 6.1.2 (current GMP is 6.3.x). This compares a GPU against a CPU, so it measures throughput per device on batched work, not a better algorithm: single-operand latency would lose to GMP. The README does not state compiler flags or the GMP build flags. A third-party report (pscamillo/mr_blackwell) says CGBN runs orders of magnitude slower than expected on Blackwell (sm_120) GPUs, and the Makefile lists architectures only up to Ampere. steleman/nvidia-cgbn is a fork adding signed integers and Blackwell support (not reported separately).
found_via: GitHub: NVlabs/CGBN, surfaced by wave-8 leads (midint enrichment) and the mr_blackwell README; README and LICENSE read via raw.githubusercontent.com, commit date from github.com/NVlabs/CGBN/commits/master

name: GNU MPFR with CUDA acceleration (CGBN backend)
baseline: GNU MPFR 4.2.1 scalar functions (mpfr_mul, mpfr_div, mpfr_sqrt, mpfr_fma, mpfr_add) with GMP 6.3.0, one CPU core
workload: Batched and device-resident correctly rounded MPFR arithmetic (mul, add, div, sqrt, fma) at precisions from 128 to 65536 bits and batch sizes 1 to 16384, GPU versus one core of the same machine running scalar MPFR; results are identical to MPFR's including rounding mode, ternary value and flags.
claimed_speedup: Peak batch speedups at n = 1024: div 30.4x and sqrt 28.2x at 32768 bits, mul 21.2x at 49152 bits, fma 18.3x at 40960 bits. Device-resident peaks at n = 16384: fma 284x at 8192 bits, mul 230x at 4096 bits, div 157x at 16384 bits, add 120x at 8192 bits, sqrt 115x at 16384 bits. A single operation is always slower (n = 1 rows are 0.0x-0.4x) and addition never wins on transfer.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc from CUDA 13.2 with NVCCFLAGS '-O3 -arch=$cuda_arch -Xcompiler -fPIC' (configure default arch 'native', sm_120 on the test GPU); host C compiler and CFLAGS for the MPFR baseline not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (sm_120, 82 SMs at 2.41 GHz, 31.4 GiB); CPU baseline is one core of the same machine, CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Optional backend enabled with --enable-cgbn; without it the library is stock MPFR 4.2.1. Needs an NVIDIA GPU and nvcc. All results in one batch must share a precision, precision above 65536 bits runs on the CPU, device access is serialized on a mutex, and GMP_NUMB_BITS must be a multiple of 32.
caveats: First-party measurements on a single machine; CPU model not given, and the baseline is one core (a multi-core MPFR would shrink the ratios by up to the core count). Single operations (n = 1) are roughly 2.5x to over 1000x slower than the CPU; division and square root above 32768 bits are slower than the CPU per the README's own Limitations section. The GitHub page shows a single commit and no history, so last_commit is the 'updated' date from the github.com/topics/arbitrary-precision-arithmetic listing (Sep 12, 2026), not a verified commit date. The tree is GNU MPFR 4.2.1 with the CUDA backend added (a fork of MPFR, whose canonical home was not opened this session, hence is_fork_of is null).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/mpfr listing, then README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: mr_blackwell (native Miller-Rabin GPU kernel)
baseline: GMP (CPU Miller-Rabin probable-prime test with GMP modular exponentiation)
workload: Base-2 Miller-Rabin probable-prime tests (Montgomery CIOS modular exponentiation, 4-bit fixed window, PTX carry chains) on 65536 random 683-bit candidates, RTX 5070 GPU versus the CPU/GMP prime-gap test on a Ryzen 9 8800X3D.
claimed_speedup: CPU (GMP) 13,700 PRP/sec versus v2d kernel 1,805,000 PRP/sec at 683 bits = 132x (README table); 295,000 PRP/sec = 21x at 1240 bits. In the prime-gap pipeline the kernel runs about 1,800,000 PRP/sec versus 13,700 for the CPU test.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_120 (Makefile), CUDA 12.9, Linux Mint; GMP version and CPU baseline build flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 5070 (SM 12.0 Blackwell) versus AMD Ryzen 9 8800X3D
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; the README says it produced 60 prime-gap world records (as of 2026-05-05) through the sethtroisi/prime-gap pipeline
tradeoffs: Specialised to Miller-Rabin / modular exponentiation of fixed-size odd moduli (template LIMBS dispatch, e.g. 22 limbs for 683 bits), not a general bigint library; NVIDIA GPUs only; drop-in replacement for the CGBN miller_rabin.h used by prime-gap.
caveats: First-party README numbers. The CPU baseline is the prime-gap gap_test_simple program, whose thread count, GMP version and flags are not stated, so the 132x is a GPU-versus-CPU ratio that may be against one core. The commits page showed no history to WebFetch, so last_commit is the 'updated' date from the github.com/topics/montgomery-multiplication listing (May 5, 2026), not a verified commit date. The CGBN-on-Blackwell slowness claim is the author's own observation.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/montgomery-multiplication listing; README and Makefile read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: APFP (arbitrary precision floating point on FPGA)
workload: Fully pipelined Karatsuba-based arbitrary precision floating-point multiplier and adder, exposed as a tiled matrix-multiplication primitive, on an Alveo U250 FPGA versus a dual-socket 36-core Xeon node running MPFR; 512-bit and 1024-bit multiplication and 512-bit matrix-matrix multiplication.
claimed_speedup: README: 2.0 GMAC/s of 512-bit matrix-matrix multiplication, 'an order of magnitude higher than a 36-core dual-socket Xeon node, corresponding to 375x CPU cores worth of throughput'.
hardware: Xilinx Alveo U250 FPGA (Vitis HLS, XRT) versus a dual-socket 36-core Xeon node (CPU model not stated in the README)
stars_or_usage: 41 stars; peer-reviewed at FCCM 2022 (ETH Zurich SPCL)
tradeoffs: Fixed precision chosen at compile time (APFP_BITS, a multiple of 512 bits, 63-bit exponent, 1-bit sign), needs Xilinx Vitis HLS and an XRT-enabled FPGA card, results exposed only through matrix-multiply kernels, not a general library.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repository root (root files: .clang-format, .gitignore, .gitmodules, CMakeLists.txt, README.md plus directories), so the code is reference only. The README does not name MPFR; the MPFR baseline comes from the FCCM'22 paper abstract, which was only seen in a search-result snippet because arXiv and the SPCL host were blocked. That snippet reports 9.8x at 4.8 GOp/s for 512-bit multiplication and 5.3x at 1.2 GOp/s for 1024-bit multiplication versus MPFR; those numbers are not verified from an opened page. The comparison is an FPGA board versus a whole 36-core CPU node, not an equal-silicon comparison; CPU model, compiler and MPFR version are not in the README. Last commit 2022-05-17 (May 2022), more than 3 years old.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/mpfr and github.com/topics/bignum?l=c%2B%2B listings; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com; paper numbers from a search result for 'Fast Arbitrary Precision Floating Point on FPGA'

name: VROOM (vectorized RNS modular multiplication, BoringSSL fork)
baseline: BoringSSL BN_mod_mul_montgomery / BN modular exponentiation and RSA, OpenSSL (separate fork harness), and FLINT 3.2.1 (GMP-based mpn_mod_mul / fmpz_mod_mul)
workload: Modular multiplication versus modulus size, modular exponentiation (public e = 65537, secret exponent, RSA-CRT) and RSA sign/verify latency using AVX-512 IFMA with a residue number system, single core pinned with taskset, versus BoringSSL Montgomery, OpenSSL and FLINT.
claimed_speedup: The README gives no figures: it says 'the relative speedup of VROOM over each baseline is the paper's claim' and points to the paper's tables (modmul sweep, modexp, RSA-CRT, RSA sign/verify). The numbers are in the USENIX Security 2026 paper (IACR ePrint 2026/393), which could not be opened this session (egress blocked), so no speedup number is recorded here.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 21.1.8 (LLVM prebuilt), CMake Release build via configure.sh (cmake -GNinja -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release), FLINT 3.2.1, run pinned with 'taskset -c 0 ./build/bssl_bench'
hardware: AWS c7i.metal-24xl, Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C (Sapphire Rapids, AVX-512 IFMA required), Amazon Linux 2023; README says relative speedups also reproduce on c7i-flex.large
stars_or_usage: 8 stars; artifact repository for a USENIX Security 2026 paper
tradeoffs: Needs a CPU with AVX-512 IFMA (the README says the RNS code path will not run without avx512ifma); research prototype built on BoringSSL BN_* routines, runtime switch via BN_MONT_CTX_set_use_rns / RSA_set_use_rns; the README warns it is not production-ready and was only tested on random inputs for selected functions.
caveats: No speedup figures appear in the repository README, so the tier A rating rests on the artifact being reproducible (public code, compiler, flags, CPU model, reproduce.sh) and on the paper's claims, which the verifier must read from the paper. Baseline columns for OpenSSL and Arkworks come from separate harnesses under baselines/ (git submodule fetched on demand). FLINT is the GMP-based baseline, not GMP itself. Fork of BoringSSL commit 3fb010b. The GPU and elliptic-curve results of the paper live in other repositories not covered here.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/residue-number-system listing, README, configure.sh and LICENSE read via raw.githubusercontent.com, commits page via github.com/kevin-he-01/vroomssl/commits/main

name: TLFloat (quad and octuple precision floating point, C++ templates)
workload: Built-in benchmark tool (cmake -DBUILD_BENCH=True), 10 s measurement per operation, TLFloat Quad versus GNU libquadmath on addition, multiplication, division, casts, compare, FMA, sqrt, rint, sin, atan, exp, log and pow.
claimed_speedup: README table (Mops/second, TLFloat vs libquadmath): addition 124.25 vs 87.7199, multiplication 102.486 vs 78.2958, FMA 68.4656 vs 1.93365, cast to/from double 168.078 vs 63.7482, compare 299.502 vs 222.788, square root 15.9095 vs 9.50421, rint 191.323 vs 37.6146, sin 2.13261 vs 1.77002. Slower than libquadmath on division (50.7983 vs 72.6179), atan (1.30394 vs 3.02089), exp (1.49075 vs 1.78973), log (1.58123 vs 1.8479) and pow (0.88467 vs 1.29873). Ratios such as FMA about 35x and addition about 1.4x are derived from page data.
stars_or_usage: 38 stars; same GitHub owner (shibatch) as SLEEF
tradeoffs: Fixed IEEE 754 binary128 and octuple precision (plus half, single, double), not arbitrary precision; constexpr-capable header library, runs on clang and MSVC where libquadmath is unavailable, also CUDA; libquadmath emulation API provided.
caveats: Mixed result, not a blanket win: slower than libquadmath on division, atan, exp, log and pow. Baseline is libquadmath, not GMP/MPFR (MPFR was not benchmarked). Numbers are first-party from TLFloat 1.11.0 (the README table predates later releases; latest release seen was v1.15.0, 2025-03-26); compiler flags not stated. last_commit is the 'updated' date from the github.com/topics/quadruple-precision listing (Aug 17, 2026), not a verified commit date.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/arbitrary-precision?l=c%2B%2B listing; README.adoc read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: mpFFT (multiprecision FFT on MPFR)
baseline: Mathematica 11.1 FFT with SetPrecision, and MATLAB 2019a with the Advanpix Multiprecision Toolbox (mp.Digits)
workload: Serial 1D complex FFT of length 1024 (random input) at 16 up to 1,048,576 decimal digits on one CPU core, and the same on 4 cores, measured as average seconds per FFT.
claimed_speedup: README: 'a more than 2x speed-up to Mathematica and a 10x speed-up to MATLAB' in serial computation with precision up to 1 million digits; 'a 10x speed-up to MATLAB' with 4 CPU cores at high precision orders (no Mathematica multicore comparison possible). The numbers are shown as plots (bench/serial_mp_N1024_time.png, bench/parallel_mp_C4_N1024_time.png).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.3.0 with -O3, statically linked MPFR 4.1.0, GMP 6.2.1, -pthread -fopenmp for parallel runs
hardware: Intel Core i5-6500 at 3.20 GHz (read from the benchmark plot title)
tradeoffs: 1D complex-to-complex, forward-only, power-of-two lengths, DIT split-radix, recursive, out-of-place, scalar code; all arithmetic comes from MPFR, so it does not beat MPFR, it beats Mathematica and Advanpix at the FFT level; the author calls the project 'still in development and far from complete'.
caveats: Baselines are proprietary systems (Mathematica 11.1, MATLAB 2019a with Advanpix) and the repository holds no scripts for them, so the comparison cannot be reproduced from the repo; the speedups are first-party and read from plots. Single i5-6500 machine, 2021 versions. Overlaps the FFT category; kept here because it is a multiprecision (MPFR-based) FFT. last_commit is the 'updated' date from the github.com/topics/multiprecision listing (Oct 10, 2021).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/multiprecision?l=c&o=desc&s=updated listing; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com; plot image downloaded from raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Unsigned Bigint (fixed-width ADX/BMI2 big integer)
workload: Add, subtract, multiply, divide (500,000 operations each) and modular exponentiation (1,000 operations) on fixed 256, 512, 1024, 2048 and 4096-bit unsigned integers, run time in the README table (units not stated).
claimed_speedup: README table (run time, lower is better), Unsigned Bigint vs boost: multiply 0.019142 vs 0.0335125 at 256 bits and 1.2972828 vs 5.5994093 at 4096 bits; modular exponentiation 0.0675292 vs 0.2627964 at 256 bits and 52.701681 vs 445.34939 at 4096 bits (about 3.9x and 8.4x, derived from page data); add and subtract 1.4x-2.4x faster. Division is slower: 0.9787682 vs 0.2175322 at 256 bits and 11.174972 vs 10.216111 at 4096 bits.
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 (build requirement); flags and Boost version not stated
hardware: CPU model not stated; needs ADX, BMI2 and RDRAND (Intel Haswell or newer, AMD Ryzen or newer)
tradeoffs: Fixed bit width chosen at compile time (unsigned_bigint<N>, N limbs of 64 bits), unsigned only, Visual Studio solution build, requires ADX, BMI2 and RDRAND, README in Chinese.
caveats: First-party table without compiler flags, CPU model, Boost version or backend (cpp_int fixed or dynamic), run-time units or the benchmark source named in the README. Division loses to Boost at every size shown. Repository has a single commit; last commit date not readable, likely 2019 (README links to the Boost 1.70 docs) so probably abandoned. Not compared against GMP.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/bignumber?l=c%2B%2B listing; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: MPLAPACK (multiple-precision BLAS/LAPACK with double-double, quad-double and CUDA backends)
baseline: GMP (mpf) and MPFR backends of the same library, at their default 512-bit precision
workload: Rgemm (multiple-precision matrix-matrix multiply) with square matrices on a Ryzen Threadripper 3970X, double-double and quad-double backends (with and without OpenMP) versus the GMP and MPFR backends, plus a CUDA double-double Rgemm on A100/V100 GPUs.
claimed_speedup: Manual section 9 peaks for Rgemm: reference GMP 19 MFlops and 693 MFlops OpenMP; reference MPFR 11 MFlops and 390 MFlops OpenMP; reference quad-double 33 MFlops and 1.3 GFlops OpenMP; reference double-double about 365 MFlops and 11.2 GFlops OpenMP. Derived from page data: double-double OpenMP is about 29x MPFR and 16x GMP, quad-double OpenMP about 3.3x MPFR and 1.9x GMP. README: CUDA double-double Rgemm and Rsyrk reach about 450 GFlops on a V100. Benchmark logs in the repo show the A100-box CUDA double-double kernel at 486,829 MFLOPS (n = 562).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.3.0 inside Docker (manual); example builds use g++ -O2, benchmark flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3970X, 256 GB DDR4-3200; GPU runs on Tesla V100 / A100 (benchmark/results/2022 folders)
tradeoffs: Faster only by giving up precision: double-double is about 32 digits (106 bits) and quad-double about 64 digits (212 bits), while the GMP and MPFR runs use 512 bits. Needs the dd/qd formats' accuracy to be enough; the library keeps one API across binary64, binary128, FP80, dd, qd, GMP and MPFR backends.
caveats: Not an equal-precision comparison: the GMP/MPFR columns are 512-bit, the dd and qd columns are 106 and 212 bits, so the speedups mostly reflect hardware double arithmetic versus software bignum. The manual itself says double results 'are not competitive to OpenBLAS or Intel MKL'. The author notes MPFR is about twice as slow as GMP, possibly because of the C++ binding copies. First-party (arXiv user manual v2.0.1, 2022) numbers; the 2023-2026 releases were not re-benchmarked in what was read. last_commit is the 'updated' date from the github.com/topics/multiple-precision listing (Sep 30, 2026).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/multiple-precision listing; README, benchmark logs (benchmark/results/2022/.../logs/log.Rgemm.*) and doc/manual/manual.pdf read via raw.githubusercontent.com
